sub_sections.title: Quality and pertinence of the project's research and innovation objectives (and the extent to which they are ambitious, and go beyond the state of the art)
sub_sections.content:
## 1.1 Quality and pertinence of the project's research and innovation objectives (and the extent to which they are ambitious, and go beyond the state of the art)

### 1.1.1 European challenge and scientific rationale

European agriculture is entering an increasingly water-constrained production environment: approximately 30% of EU territory is affected by seasonal water scarcity in an average year, while climate change is expected to intensify drought frequency and severity and to increase both the agricultural area requiring irrigation and irrigation demand in already-irrigated areas. This exposure is most acute for high-value horticultural field crops, for which inappropriate irrigation timing directly affects productivity, fruit quality, water-use efficiency and economic return. FIELDWISE takes processing tomato as its model crop precisely because it is a demanding predictive-irrigation system: crop productivity depends strongly on the temporal interaction between water availability, atmospheric demand, developmental stage and irrigation management. The project is therefore pertinent to a concrete, quantified European problem rather than to a generic monitoring task, and its scientific pertinence is anchored in a single central question — whether physiologically grounded crop water stress in high-value processing tomato can be forecast early enough to support irrigation decisions while maintaining reliable predictive performance as the model moves from historical experimental observations to unseen seasons, from Hungary to Bulgaria, and ultimately from research fields to commercial farming conditions.

This question exposes a structural weakness in current agricultural AI. The rapid expansion of Earth Observation, proximal sensing, IoT and machine learning has enabled increasingly sophisticated crop-monitoring systems, yet agricultural ML remains predominantly evaluated through retrospective metrics (R², RMSE, F1-score, classification accuracy). A model can achieve impressive retrospective performance while being unsuitable for actual irrigation management: observations from related seasons, plots or fields may appear in both training and testing (optimistic estimates); a model may learn environment-specific relationships tied to a particular soil, cultivar, management regime or year rather than transferable crop–water relationships; accurate identification of an already-established stress condition may arrive too late to change the irrigation decision; and even a model that transfers between research experiments may fail under the heterogeneity and incomplete data of commercial farming. FIELDWISE therefore reframes the field's objective from retrospective accuracy toward prospective prediction, transferability, and field-level decision value.

### 1.1.2 Research and innovation objectives (measurable and verifiable)

The project pursues six research and innovation objectives, each attached to a defined measurable output and each verified by named deliverables produced within the 30-month action (a 24-month European Fellowship at the host, months 1–24, plus a 6-month non-academic placement, months 25–30). The objectives, their canonical measurable targets, and their verification instruments are:

- **O1 — Construct a harmonised five-year MATE soil-plant-atmosphere dataset.** Measurable target: *QC-controlled historical database and documented metadata*. Verified by the deliverables *Harmonised historical database* (month 6) and *Data/target/validation protocol* (month 6). This objective is realistically achievable because the underlying five-year archive already exists; the work is harmonisation, quality control and leakage-safe target/validation design, not new multi-year data collection.

- **O2 — Identify physiologically meaningful hyperspectral early-warning signatures and establish their Sentinel-2 transferability.** Measurable target: *Validated hyperspectral/Sentinel-compatible feature library*. Verified by the *Physiological validation dataset* (month 14) and the *Hyperspectral-to-Sentinel transfer library* (month 14). Verifiability is explicit: the output is a documented feature library whose transferability to Sentinel-2 resolution is testable.

- **O3 — Develop prospective uncertainty-aware crop water-stress forecasts.** Measurable target: *Calibrated forecasts at actionable horizons*. Verified by the *Comparative modelling benchmark* (month 18) and the *FIELDWISE predictive engine/model card* (month 18). Measurability rests on calibration and lead-time being reported quantities, not on accuracy alone.

- **O4 — Quantify temporal and Hungary->Bulgaria geographic transferability and evaluate adaptation.** Measurable target: *Independent transferability benchmark*. Verified by the *Temporal transferability benchmark* (month 21), the *Hungary->Bulgaria transferability report* (month 21) and the *Adaptation protocol* (month 21). The benchmark is independent by construction, using an out-of-country evaluation environment.

- **O5 — Quantify research->commercial-field operational transferability.** Measurable target: *AgroVIR farmer-field evaluation*. Verified by the *Commercial-field transferability assessment* (month 30) and the *Field Decision Value report* (month 30).

- **O6 — Translate validated predictions into irrigation priority and a functional web MVP.** Measurable target: *DrR web MVP + Field Decision Value + AgroVIR requirements assessment*. Verified by the *DrR web MVP* (month 24), the *AgroVIR functional/technical evaluation* (month 30) and the *FMIS integration roadmap* (month 30).

The objectives are decomposed into seven research questions (RQ1–RQ7) and six falsifiable hypotheses (H1–H6), which sharpen their measurability. Several hypotheses are deliberately framed as expected performance degradations to be *quantified* rather than as optimistic claims to be confirmed: H3 predicts that unseen-season performance will fall below conventional random-validation performance, revealing the extent of temporal generalisation; H4 predicts a geographic performance drop from Hungary to Bulgaria that limited local calibration or hierarchical modelling can partly recover; H5 predicts further degradation moving from research to farmer-managed fields; and H6 predicts that the model with the highest retrospective accuracy will not necessarily provide the greatest irrigation decision value. This construction makes the objectives genuinely verifiable — each can fail — and directly counters the optimistic-evaluation pathology the project critiques. Six explicitly stated scientific gaps (G1 physiological-target, G2 sensor-domain, G3 temporal, G4 geographic-transferability, G5 operational-transferability, G6 decision-value) map one-to-one onto the objectives, so that no objective is asserted without a stated deficiency in the current state of the art that it closes.

### 1.1.3 Ambition and advance beyond the state of the art

The project's ambition is expressed as six deliberate transitions that each move an established practice to a more demanding one: spectral proxy → physiological target; hyperspectral discovery → satellite scaling; static detection → prospective prediction; internal validation → temporal transferability; single-country modelling → geographic transferability; and research accuracy → commercial-field decision value. Three advances are especially distinctive against the state of the art. First, FIELDWISE defines water stress through physiologically meaningful plant responses rather than relying solely on vegetation-index thresholds, replacing spectral-proxy stress definitions with a physiologically grounded target. Second, it establishes a methodological bridge from high-information proximal hyperspectral observation to scalable Sentinel-2 prediction, explicitly investigating which proximal stress signatures survive spectral resampling and scale-aware calibration — a step beyond systems that either stay proximal or start from satellite indices. Third, it introduces Field Decision Value (FDV) as a final evaluation layer, so that models are selected by field-level irrigation usefulness (lead time, calibration, avoided false/missed interventions) rather than by retrospective accuracy alone; this reframes what "the best agricultural model" means and is the conceptual core of the proposal's title, *Beyond Prediction Accuracy*.

Ambition is also structural, not merely conceptual. The transferability question is pursued through a four-stage validation ladder — scientific development and validation on the primary Hungarian data environment, an independent cross-country transferability test in Bulgaria, operational transferability under commercial farmer-field conditions, and a research-to-operation delivery step through the *DrR web MVP*. Very few agricultural-AI studies subject a single model to this full chain from plant physiology to satellite observation, across two countries, and across the research-to-commercial boundary; doing so is what allows FIELDWISE to convert transferability from an untested assumption into measured evidence. The five work packages instantiate this ambition end-to-end: WP1 *Historical Data and Target Design*, WP2 *Physiological Early Warning and Hyperspectral-to-Sentinel Transfer*, WP3 *Prospective and Uncertainty-Aware Prediction*, WP4 *Temporal and Cross-Country Transferability*, and WP5 *Operational Transfer, Decision Value and Web MVP*, with a dependency chain (WP1→WP2→WP3→WP4→WP5) that carries the harmonised target design through to the externally evaluated operational demonstrator.

### 1.1.4 Realistic achievability and de-risking

The objectives are ambitious but achievable within the fellowship. The programme does not begin from a conceptual base: the researcher has already initiated *DrR - Digital Agronomist*, a desktop research prototype that demonstrates the technical feasibility of integrating soil-sensor, field-meteorological and Sentinel-2 data in a common digital environment. FIELDWISE does not fund the conversion of that prototype into a website; it supplies the missing scientific validation and transferability framework — physiologically validated targets, prospective and uncertainty-aware forecasting, cross-year robustness, cross-country and research-to-commercial transferability, decision value and operational interoperability — that the prototype has not yet established. Because the five-year data archive already exists and the prototype already integrates the relevant data streams, the principal risks are scientific (whether signatures transfer, whether forecasts remain useful) rather than infrastructural, and the work is sequenced so that each objective's output is validated before the next depends on it. Early, verifiable deliverables (the harmonised database and the data/target/validation protocol at month 6) front-load the leakage-safe foundations on which every later transferability claim rests, and the operational demonstrator (*DrR web MVP*, month 24) is completed before the placement so that the placement is validation and transfer rather than first build.

Finally, the design is explicitly self-corrective and responsive to prior review. Its architecture answers a previous submission's identified weakness in the methodological treatment of heterogeneous spatial, spectral and temporal information; its work plan introduces corrective decision points during the action to address an earlier criticism that milestones occurred too late to enable corrective action; and its exploitation and IP route through commercial-field evaluation responds to an earlier criticism that the route to users and the IP strategy were insufficiently substantiated. Taken together, the objectives are quality-controlled, pertinent to a quantified European challenge, individually measurable and verifiable through named deliverables, ambitious in the transitions they attempt, and realistically achievable on an existing data and prototype foundation.

sub_sections.title: Soundness of the proposed methodology (including interdisciplinary approaches, consideration of the gender dimension and other diversity aspects if relevant for the research project, and the quality of open science practices)
sub_sections.content:
## 1.2 Soundness of the proposed methodology (including interdisciplinary approaches, consideration of the gender dimension and other diversity aspects if relevant for the research project, and the quality of open science practices)

### 1.2.1 Overall methodology: concepts, models and assumptions

The methodological core of FIELDWISE is a single, coherent design principle: a predictive crop-water-stress capability is only scientifically credible if it is evaluated the way it will be used, and is therefore built and tested along a graded chain of increasingly demanding validation rather than optimised against a retrospective accuracy metric. The overall methodology instantiates this principle as a four-stage validation ladder — scientific development and validation on the primary Hungarian data environment (MATE), an independent cross-country transferability test in Bulgaria (MVCRI), operational transferability under commercial farmer-field conditions (AgroVIR), and a research-to-operation delivery step through the *DrR web MVP*. The five work packages are the operational form of this ladder: WP1 *Historical Data and Target Design*, WP2 *Physiological Early Warning and Hyperspectral-to-Sentinel Transfer*, WP3 *Prospective and Uncertainty-Aware Prediction*, WP4 *Temporal and Cross-Country Transferability*, and WP5 *Operational Transfer, Decision Value and Web MVP*, connected by the dependency chain WP1→WP2→WP3, WP1→WP3, WP2→WP3, WP3→WP4 and WP3/WP4→WP5. This is a single-researcher action: the fellow executes every work package, and this is what makes the methodology integrative by construction rather than by hand-off.

The methodology rests on four explicit modelling concepts. First, a *physiologically grounded stress target*: water stress is defined through physiologically meaningful plant responses rather than through vegetation-index thresholds alone, so that the quantity the models predict is biologically interpretable (task *Establish physiological stress definition*, WP1). Second, a *leakage-safe validation design* established before any model is trained (task *Establish leakage-safe validation design*, WP1), which forbids observations from related seasons, plots or fields appearing simultaneously in training and testing and thereby prevents the optimistic performance estimates that the field's accuracy-centred evaluation routinely produces. Third, a *sensor-domain bridge* from high-information proximal hyperspectral observation to scalable Sentinel-2 prediction, built from spectral-response resampling, concurrent proximal/satellite observation and spatial-scale calibration (WP2), which asks specifically which physiological signatures survive resampling to Sentinel-2 spectral and spatial resolution. Fourth, a *prospective, uncertainty-aware forecasting* layer: temporal feature engineering feeds a graded model portfolio — transparent baseline models, random-forest/XGBoost models, and Bayesian/hierarchical models — with multi-horizon forecasting, probability calibration and uncertainty quantification, and feature ablation and error analysis (WP3), so that the system outputs calibrated forecasts at actionable lead times rather than a single point classification of an already-established condition.

The assumptions that underpin the work are stated as six falsifiable hypotheses, several of which are deliberately framed as performance degradations to be *quantified* rather than as optimistic claims to be confirmed. H1 assumes that combining soil-water availability and atmospheric demand with hyperspectral crop-response information identifies developing stress before substantial canopy-greenness deterioration; H2 assumes that a subset of physiologically meaningful hyperspectral features can be translated into Sentinel-compatible predictors through resampling, concurrent observation and scale-aware calibration; H3 assumes unseen-season performance will fall below conventional random-validation performance; H4 assumes a Hungary→Bulgaria performance drop that limited local calibration and/or hierarchical modelling can partly recover; H5 assumes further degradation moving from research to farmer-managed fields; and H6 assumes that the highest-accuracy model will not necessarily deliver the greatest irrigation decision value. Because each hypothesis can fail, the methodology is genuinely testable, and the final evaluation layer — the *Field Decision Value* (FDV) framework (WP5) — makes the selection criterion itself an object of study, selecting models by field-level irrigation usefulness (lead time, calibration, avoided false/missed interventions) rather than by retrospective accuracy.

A further underpinning assumption is that the empirical foundation already exists: the approximately five-year MATE soil-plant-atmosphere archive is harmonised and quality-controlled rather than newly collected, and the *DrR - Digital Agronomist* desktop research prototype already demonstrates integration of soil-sensor, field-meteorological and Sentinel-2 data in a common digital environment. This means the principal residual uncertainties are scientific (whether signatures transfer, whether forecasts remain useful) rather than infrastructural, which is what makes the ladder tractable within a 30-month action.

### 1.2.2 How the methodology delivers the objectives

The methodology maps one-to-one onto the six research and innovation objectives, and each mapping is closed by named deliverables. WP1 delivers O1 (*Construct a harmonised five-year MATE soil-plant-atmosphere dataset*) through the *Harmonised historical database* and the *Data/target/validation protocol*, both due in month 6, which front-load the leakage-safe foundations on which every later transferability claim depends. WP2 delivers O2 (*Identify physiologically meaningful hyperspectral early-warning signatures and establish their Sentinel-2 transferability*) through the *Physiological validation dataset* and the *Hyperspectral-to-Sentinel transfer library*, both due in month 14. WP3 delivers O3 (*Develop prospective uncertainty-aware crop water-stress forecasts*) through the *Comparative modelling benchmark* and the *FIELDWISE predictive engine/model card*, both due in month 18. WP4 delivers O4 (*Quantify temporal and Hungary->Bulgaria geographic transferability and evaluate adaptation*) through the *Temporal transferability benchmark*, the *Hungary->Bulgaria transferability report* and the *Adaptation protocol*, all due in month 21. WP5 delivers O5 (*Quantify research->commercial-field operational transferability*) and O6 (*Translate validated predictions into irrigation priority and a functional web MVP*) through the *DrR web MVP* (due month 24) and, at month 30, the *Commercial-field transferability assessment*, the *Field Decision Value report*, the *AgroVIR functional/technical evaluation* and the *FMIS integration roadmap*. Because the modelling method is validated before the next stage depends on it — leakage-safe design before modelling, cross-country transfer before operational transfer, a built MVP (month 24) before the non-academic placement (months 25–30) — the sequence guarantees that the operational-transfer conclusions rest on scientifically validated evidence and not on optimistic extrapolation.

### 1.2.3 Key methodological challenges and mitigation

Five methodological challenges are identified in the design, each with a mitigation that is built into the work plan rather than deferred. (1) *Data leakage and optimistic estimation.* The dominant risk in agricultural ML is that related seasons, plots or fields contaminate the train/test split. Mitigation: the leakage-safe validation design is a month-6 deliverable (*Data/target/validation protocol*) that constrains all downstream modelling, and temporal generalisation is measured directly through leave-one-year-out validation (WP4). (2) *Sensor-domain scale gap.* It is not guaranteed that proximal hyperspectral stress signatures survive resampling to Sentinel-2 resolution. Mitigation: concurrent hyperspectral/Sentinel observations and spatial-scale calibration (WP2), with the outcome recorded transparently as a per-feature *Hyperspectral-to-Sentinel transfer library* so that a partial result is a documented finding rather than a hidden failure. (3) *Limited sample size and temporal density.* Mitigation: a graded model portfolio that begins with transparent baselines and introduces more complex Bayesian/hierarchical or deep architectures only where sample size and temporal density justify them, keeping model complexity proportionate to the evidence. (4) *Cross-country transfer failure.* A Hungarian-trained model may encode site-specific relationships. Mitigation: an explicit zero-shot Hungary→Bulgaria transfer, a geographic transferability-gap assessment, limited Bulgarian calibration and hierarchical/Bayesian adaptation (WP4), with the *Adaptation protocol* quantifying how much local information is required to recover performance. (5) *Commercial-field heterogeneity and incomplete data.* A model that transfers between research experiments may still fail under farmer-managed conditions. Mitigation: operational transfer to AgroVIR farmer field(s) and quantification of research→commercial transferability (WP5), identifying which inputs and model components are robust enough for operational use, with the FDV framework ensuring that the model finally recommended is the one most useful for irrigation decisions, not the one with the highest retrospective accuracy. This architecture directly answers a previous submission's identified weakness in the methodological treatment of heterogeneous spatial, spectral and temporal information.

### 1.2.4 Integration of methods and disciplines

An interdisciplinary approach is intrinsic to the project and is not optional: the central research question runs from plant physiology, through proximal and satellite remote sensing, through machine learning and uncertainty quantification, to operational agricultural decision support, and no single discipline can answer it. The methodology therefore integrates six method families. Plant physiology and horticultural crop science supply the physiologically grounded stress target and the processing-tomato experimental system (contributed through MATE, the primary experimental and data environment). Remote sensing, hyperspectral imaging and field spectroscopy supply the early-warning signatures and the sensor-domain bridge; this is the disciplinary home of the supervisor, Prof. András Jung, whose expertise is in remote sensing, hyperspectral imaging and field spectroscopy, and geoinformatics. Geoinformatics and Earth Observation supply the Sentinel-2 scaling and reproducible geospatial computation. Machine learning, meta-modelling and agro-meteorology supply the prospective, uncertainty-aware modelling and its quality assurance; this is the disciplinary home of the co-supervisor, Dr. Roland Hollós, whose expertise is in machine learning and meta-modelling of crop and grassland multi-model outputs and in agro-meteorology, and who provides the methodological lead and quality assurance for model development and testing. Software and operational information-systems engineering supply the research-to-operation translation and the FMIS interoperability assessment (contributed through AgroVIR).

Integration is realised through three concrete mechanisms rather than asserted. First, structurally: because the fellow — a plant physiologist extending into geospatial data science — personally executes all five work packages, the biological definition of the target, its spectral representation, its predictive modelling and its operational evaluation are carried through by one integrating agent, and the fellowship's two-way transfer of knowledge (crop physiology and agronomy into the host; geoinformatics, EO time-series analysis, Bayesian hierarchical modelling and uncertainty quantification into the fellow) is the disciplinary bridge. Second, through supervision: the division of methodological responsibility — the fellow designing, building and running the models, the co-supervisor quality-assuring the model development and testing, and the supervisor providing the remote-sensing and geoinformatics lead — binds the physiological, geospatial and machine-learning strands at the point of method design. Third, through governance: the Project Steering Group brings the host and the three partners (MATE, MVCRI, AgroVIR) into a common decision structure at defined review points, so that the source-domain data environment, the cross-country transfer environment and the operational environment are coordinated against the same milestones. The disciplinary integration is thus embedded in who does the work, who assures it, and how the partners are coordinated.

### 1.2.5 Gender dimension and other diversity aspects

Consistent with the guidance that this question concerns the *content* of the planned research and innovation activities and not gender balance in the team, a biological sex or gender dimension is not relevant to the core research content of FIELDWISE, and a justification is provided. The subject of study is a plant crop — processing tomato — and its physiological water-stress response as observed through soil, meteorological, hyperspectral and satellite data and modelled with machine learning. There is no human or animal subject in the modelled system, and neither the physiological stress target, the spectral features, nor the predictive models contain a variable for which human sex or gender is an analytically meaningful factor. Introducing a gender variable into the crop-physiology or Earth-observation content would therefore be artificial rather than sound.

Other diversity aspects are, however, addressed where they are genuinely relevant to the research content. The methodology is explicitly built around *agro-environmental and geographic diversity*: the model is developed in one European agro-climate (Hungary, MATE) and deliberately transferred to a contrasting one (Bulgaria, MVCRI), and then from research fields to commercially managed farmer fields (AgroVIR). This diversity of environments is not incidental — it is the mechanism by which the project distinguishes transferable crop–water relationships from site-specific artefacts, and the MVCRI role is specifically a Hungary→Bulgaria transferability test rather than a means of enlarging the sample. Where human participants do enter the research content — the structured usability and interoperability feedback collected from AgroVIR staff and participating farmers in WP5 — the design applies informed consent and a right of withdrawal, collects no health, biometric or special-category data, and reports results only in aggregated or anonymised form; inclusive and representative engagement of the participating end-users is the appropriate diversity consideration at that point. Personal data (farm contact details and field boundaries tied to a named holding) and commercially sensitive farmer data (yields, irrigation records, field geometries) are handled under data minimisation, review by the host's Data Protection Officer, and a data-sharing agreement, which is both an ethics and a diversity-of-stakeholder safeguard on the research content.

### 1.2.6 Open science practices and research data management

Open science is implemented as an integral part of the methodology under the principle "as open as possible, as closed as necessary", consistent with the call's requirement that training and research activities foster an open-science culture, knowledge valorisation and good scientific conduct including research integrity. The methodology produces open outputs by design rather than as an afterthought: the harmonisation protocols and documented metadata of the *Harmonised historical database*; the *Data/target/validation protocol* including the validation split manifests that make the leakage-safe design reproducible; the hyperspectral-to-Sentinel methodology and the *Hyperspectral-to-Sentinel transfer library*; analysis and model code where intellectual property permits; the model card accompanying the *FIELDWISE predictive engine/model card*; FAIR metadata; selected derived or anonymised datasets; and open-access publications built around the project's principal scientific outputs. Reproducibility is further supported by pre-registered measurement protocols for the cross-country work at MVCRI and by transparent baseline models and documented feature-ablation and error analysis in the modelling work package. Open-science engagement — open-access publication, code and model cards where IP permits, FAIR metadata and validation split manifests — is also a named component of the *Career Development Plan* (agreed by month 3), so that the practice is trained as well as executed.

Research data management is treated as a first-class methodological instrument. A Data Management Plan will be produced as an early project deliverable by month 6, aligned with the harmonised database and the data/target/validation protocol, defining for each data class its FAIR handling, access conditions, retention and licensing. The plan makes explicit the boundary between open and restricted outputs: Copernicus/Sentinel-2 inputs and the project's own methodological and derived-data outputs are opened to the fullest extent compatible with intellectual-property constraints, while personal data held by the *DrR web MVP* and commercially sensitive farmer data from AgroVIR are protected under GDPR-compliant minimisation, data-sharing agreements and aggregated or anonymised publication. Two known constraints are stated honestly rather than glossed: some code is subject to the background intellectual property of the pre-existing *DrR - Digital Agronomist* components, and some farmer-supplied data is commercially sensitive; in both cases the "as closed as necessary" qualifier is invoked deliberately and the corresponding methodology, metadata and anonymised derivatives are opened even where the raw asset cannot be. This yields an open-science posture that maximises reuse and reproducibility of the scientific method while remaining compliant with data-protection and IP obligations.

sub_sections.title: Quality of the supervision, training and of the two-way transfer of knowledge between the researcher and the host
sub_sections.content:
## 1.3 Quality of the supervision, training and of the two-way transfer of knowledge between the researcher and the host

### 1.3.1 Qualifications and experience of the supervisory team

FIELDWISE is supervised at Eötvös Loránd University (ELTE) by a two-person team whose combined expertise spans exactly the disciplinary distance the fellowship asks the researcher to travel — from plant physiology into scalable geospatial prediction and operational decision support — reinforced by a third, advisory strand at the primary experimental environment. The supervision architecture is therefore matched to the project's own interdisciplinary claim (§1.2): no single supervisor could quality-assure a chain that runs from a physiologically grounded stress target, through hyperspectral-to-Sentinel scaling, to uncertainty-aware forecasting and field-level decision value.

The lead supervisor is Prof. András Jung, Professor at ELTE's Faculty of Informatics, Institute of Cartography and Geoinformatics, whose research is in remote sensing, hyperspectral imaging and field spectroscopy, and geoinformatics. His expertise falls directly on the project's methodological core — the sensor-domain bridge from high-information proximal hyperspectral observation to scalable Sentinel-2 prediction, which is the heart of WP2. His current output evidences an active, recent Earth-observation and agricultural-monitoring track record: three 2025 peer-reviewed articles on agricultural lighting and Daily Light Integral mapping and on remote-sensing-based monitoring of agricultural land-use intensity, each verified against the publisher record for its DOI, together with a 2024 methodological contribution on deep-learning vectorisation that evidences method breadth. This is a line of work adjacent to — rather than identical with — the crop-stress remote sensing FIELDWISE needs, which is precisely why the fellow benefits: the supervisor supplies the scaling, spectroscopy and geoinformatics competence she does not yet hold, while the biological definition of the target comes from her. Prof. Jung chairs the Project Steering Group and is the standing escalation point for scientific-method decisions and for the training plan, giving the action a single accountable senior lead across its full 30 months. (ELTE records a temporary deputy directorship of the institute; consistent with that being an incidental post, he is described here by his professorship.)

The co-supervisor is Dr. Roland Hollós, of the ELTE Department of Meteorology, whose expertise is in machine learning and meta-modelling of crop and grassland multi-model outputs and in agro-meteorology. He holds the methodological lead and quality assurance for model development and testing: the fellow designs, builds and runs the models, and Dr. Hollós quality-assures them. His responsibility concentrates on the prospective, uncertainty-aware modelling of WP3 Prospective and Uncertainty-Aware Prediction and on the transferability evaluation of WP4 Temporal and Cross-Country Transferability — the two work packages where the project's most demanding methodological claims (calibration, lead time, temporal and Hungary→Bulgaria generalisation) are tested. Because he sits in a different ELTE department from the hosting institute, the supervision is genuinely interdisciplinary within the beneficiary rather than a single-group arrangement, and his primary employment is at ELTE with his supervision under this action carried out at the beneficiary, satisfying the MSCA requirement that supervision be provided at the host.

A second, personal supervision strand is provided at MATE by Prof. Gábor Milics, full professor and Hungary's country representative to the International Society of Precision Agriculture, who works on remote sensing in precision agriculture and advises the fellow directly. He held the same advisory role in the fellow's prior MSCA-PF application and continues in it for FIELDWISE, adding an agronomy-facing remote-sensing perspective alongside the two ELTE supervisors.

On hosting experience the proposal is deliberately candid: ELTE has not previously hosted a funded MSCA fellow. What is nonetheless already established, rather than untested, is the supervisory relationship itself — the same fellow and the same lead supervisor at ELTE prepared a prior MSCA-PF application (PLANTDIGISENSE, HORIZON-MSCA-2025-PF), which scored 70.40% against the 70.00% threshold. FIELDWISE is therefore a considered resubmission by an established fellow–supervisor pairing that must move a score rather than repair a broken relationship, and the supervision, host arrangements and research concept are already worked through. In this the fellowship also delivers the call's expected outcome of enhanced quality and sustainability of research training and supervision at the participating organisation (EO-05).

### 1.3.2 Planned training activities

Training is organised through a Career Development Plan, delivered as project deliverable Career Development Plan and agreed by month 3. The call requires the plan to be established jointly by supervisor(s) and researcher; with a co-supervisor in place, joint establishment means both supervisors and the fellow sign it. It is reviewed at the project's five steering points across the action, so that the training programme is actively steered rather than fixed once at the start. The plan integrates scientific, management and transferable-skills training.

**Scientific training.** Eleven host-to-fellow competences are delivered as supervised practice plus named ELTE courses: geoinformatics; EO time-series analysis; optical/SAR integration; hyperspectral-to-multispectral transfer; spatio-temporal modelling; Bayesian hierarchical modelling; uncertainty quantification; transfer learning/domain adaptation; reproducible geospatial computation; research software/web deployment; and IP and research exploitation. These map precisely onto the competence gap the fellow's profile leaves open — Bayesian and spatio-temporal modelling, sensor-domain transfer, uncertainty, domain adaptation and decision evaluation — so the scientific-training content is derived from a diagnosed need rather than assembled generically.

**Transferable and management skills.** Seven strands are trained: research integrity; open science and FAIR practice; generative-AI literacy; grant writing; IP and exploitation; project management; and science communication. This directly satisfies the call's requirement (SR-04) that training integrate key transferable skills and competences, including digital skills such as generative AI, and foster an open-science culture, knowledge valorisation and good scientific conduct including research integrity.

**Teaching and knowledge feedback into education.** Research results feed back into host teaching through two measures: co-design and delivery of a full module unit within an ELTE MSc course on Earth observation for agriculture, and co-supervision of the field-experiment component of one PhD student's work. Because the fellow already has five years of university teaching (syllabus design, lecturing and examining in Bulgarian and English, and Bachelor's thesis supervision), the teaching component is framed as the transfer of an existing strength into a new discipline, a new institution and a new language of instruction, and the step up towards doctoral-level supervision — contributing to the call outcomes on research results feeding into teaching and on knowledge circulation from research into education (EO-08, EO-06).

**Publications and open science.** The publications plan targets four principal scientific outputs (P1–P4) with at least two high-quality peer-reviewed submissions during or shortly after the fellowship, and open-science engagement is itself a trained competence — open-access publication, code and model cards where IP permits, FAIR metadata and validation split manifests — so the open-science practices described in §1.2 are executed and learned rather than merely promised.

**Supervision cadence.** Training is underpinned by a defined cadence: a weekly one-to-one between the fellow and the lead supervisor; a weekly technical session with the co-supervisor concentrated on the modelling and transferability work packages (WP3 and WP4), tapering thereafter; a monthly written progress record held by the fellow; and a quarterly review against the Career Development Plan attended by both supervisors. This makes supervision continuous and documented rather than event-driven.

### 1.3.3 Two-way transfer of knowledge between researcher and host

FIELDWISE is a European Fellowship, based on an intra-EU move of the researcher from Bulgaria to Hungary; the relevant knowledge transfer is therefore two-way, between the researcher and the host, and not the three-way transfer required of a Global Fellowship's outgoing phase. The exchange is genuinely bidirectional, along the axis crop physiology/agronomy ↔ geospatial/data science.

**Host → researcher.** ELTE transfers to the fellow the eleven scientific competences listed above, converting a plant physiologist into a scientist who can build, validate and scale geospatial predictive models — the core of the intended career progression from plant physiologist/agronomist to EO/geospatial crop scientist to an independent researcher in transferable agricultural intelligence.

**Researcher → host.** The fellow brings into the ELTE remote-sensing group competences the host does not itself hold: plant physiology; horticultural crop science; plant protection/agronomy; water-stress experimentation; physiological phenotyping; hyperspectral field measurements; biological interpretation of Earth observation; the preliminary development of the DrR - Digital Agronomist prototype; and access to complementary agricultural research collaborations. This is a substantive contribution to the host, not a courtesy: it supplies the biologically grounded stress target and the physiological interpretation that turn the group's Earth-observation methods from spectral-proxy monitoring into a physiologically meaningful prediction problem, and it strengthens the host's R&I capacity and knowledge-transfer capability (EO-07).

The two-way exchange between fellow and host is amplified, but not replaced, by the associated-partner structure, which extends it into a genuine academic–research–industry knowledge chain: MATE provides the long-term experimental knowledge and source-domain dataset; MVCRI provides the independent Bulgarian research environment for a Hungary→Bulgaria transferability test rather than merely a larger sample; and AgroVIR provides the bridge from research field to farmer field and from research prototype to operational requirements. The action does not rely on a separate secondment; its inter-institutional and cross-country exposure is delivered through these associated partners and through the non-academic placement described below, keeping the fellow's own supervised research time at the host intact.

### 1.3.4 Rationale and added value of the non-academic placement

The action includes a non-academic placement at AgroVIR, the applicable inter-sectoral element under the call's optional provision for a non-academic sector placement of up to six months at the end of the project (SR-06). It runs for the final six months of the 30-month action (months 25–30), after the 24-month European Fellowship phase at ELTE. Sequencing is deliberate: the DrR web MVP is delivered by month 24, before the placement begins, so that the placement is validation and operational transfer rather than first build.

**Added value for the project.** The placement makes the operational-transfer half of the proposal structural rather than asserted. The project's own gap and hypothesis on operational transferability (G5/H5) hold that research-to-farm transfer is where models break under commercial heterogeneity and incomplete data; a six-month period embedded in the company that runs the farms is the strongest available evidence that the proposal takes its own gap seriously. It also directly answers the criticism recorded against the previous submission — that the economic and technological route to users, and the IP strategy, were insufficiently substantiated — by routing the exploitation and decision-value evidence through a real commercial operator.

**Added value for the researcher.** The placement supplies the inter-sectoral half of the intended career progression — operational AI evaluation, research-to-MVP translation and first-hand exposure to commercial agricultural-software requirements — none of which the academic host can provide, since ELTE is the methodological and training environment and its own capacity is research infrastructure. This is the segment of the researcher's profile that makes her employable in precision-agriculture, irrigation-technology and FMIS companies as well as in academia, and it embodies the new inter-sectoral mind-set the call seeks (EO-02).

**Why it must be inside the company, and why six months.** The placement's work content is four items that each depend on the company's own operational environment: operational hardening of the prediction pipeline in a production FMIS environment; the nine-dimension operational assessment producing the AgroVIR functional/technical evaluation; the FMIS integration roadmap written from inside the implementing company; and requirements engineering and user testing with commercial growers. These deepen existing WP5 Operational Transfer, Decision Value and Web MVP content rather than adding a new strand, and they cannot be executed from outside the firm — a production FMIS environment, commercial engineering practice and direct contact with paying growers are precisely what the academic host cannot supply. The six-month ceiling is used in full to accommodate an operational assessment and a requirements process that must run over a real cropping and product cycle.

**Placement supervision and hosting.** On-site supervision during the placement is provided by a named on-site supervisor, Miklós Maróti, at senior research grade; the research-side seniority of the on-site supervisor keeps the placement in a training register rather than a purely commercial-engineering one, which is what an MSCA placement requires. The fellow is provided with desk or office space at AgroVIR for the placement period and with access to the FMIS development and staging environment and to the customer-data environment — the two systems on which the placement's work content actually runs — and is embedded in the AgroVIR team responsible for the FMIS platform. (The identity and grade of the on-site supervisor, the precise hosting arrangements and the composition of the team the fellow joins rest on host-supplied information still to be confirmed by AgroVIR before submission; they are stated here because, per the Guide for Applicants, the non-academic placement is described in Part B-1 and assessed for relevance and quality under this criterion, and are not yet independently evidenced.)

sub_sections.title: Quality and appropriateness of the researcher's professional experience, competences and skills
sub_sections.content:
## 1.4 Quality and appropriateness of the researcher's professional experience, competences and skills

### 1.4.1 A profile whose scientific core is the project's scientific core

The applicant, Dr. Rositsa Cholakova — who published before 2020 under the name Rositsa Cholakova-Bimbalova, a change noted here because her early record is filed under the earlier form — is a plant physiologist whose existing professional experience is matched to the disciplinary core on which FIELDWISE is built. The project's central object is a *physiologically grounded* water-stress target (§1.1, §1.2), and the applicant's research career is precisely in plant stress physiology. She holds a 2020 doctorate in Plant Physiology from Agricultural University – Plovdiv (Faculty of Agronomy, Department of Plant Physiology and Biochemistry; professional field 6.1 Agronomy), supervised by Prof. Dr. Andon Vassilev, on the low-temperature stress response of maize and the effectiveness of subsequent foliar fertilisation. She served as Assistant Professor in Plant Physiology and Plant Stress Physiology at Agricultural University – Plovdiv (2015–2020) and is now Chief Assistant Professor and plant-physiology researcher at Maritsa Vegetable Crops Research Institute. Her first-author publications from this period — for example in *Acta Agrobotanica* (2019) and in the *CBU International Conference Proceedings* (2017, with Vassilev), both under Cholakova-Bimbalova — evidence a genuine, peer-reviewed track record in exactly the plant-stress-physiology domain that supplies the project's biological definition of the stress event. This foundation is what makes her the appropriate person to define a stress target that is biologically interpretable rather than a spectral proxy: the competence the project's novelty rests on is one she already holds.

That foundation is horticultural as well as physiological, which is appropriate to a processing-tomato action. Her MSc Plant Protection and BSc Plant Protection (both Agricultural University – Plovdiv) and her work as a specialist consultant to farmers on physiological monitoring and integrated plant protection place her competence in the agronomy of high-value field crops, not in physiology in the abstract. Her current and recent projects converge on the FIELDWISE crop and stress directly: she is a participant in ZEMDKT 17 (2024–2026), whose Task 7 addresses abiotic stress — drought and salinity — in *Solanum lycopersicum*, and in the HORIZON-MSCA-2025-SE-01-01 SolGenSys action (2026–2030) on tomato multi-stress tolerance. She therefore comes to the fellowship already working on tomato water/abiotic stress, so the source-domain science is her existing subject matter and not a new field she must learn.

### 1.4.2 Emerging geospatial and data-science competence, stated honestly

The second half of the FIELDWISE profile — Earth observation, geospatial computation and machine learning — is one in which the applicant is credibly and demonstrably *transitioning*, and the proposal describes the maturity of this half honestly rather than overstating it. Her publication record of nine items is overwhelmingly in plant physiology; only three items touch remote sensing, all dated 2025 or later and all with the applicant as a middle author. The proposal does not therefore rest her Earth-observation competence on a publication record it does not yet have. Instead, that competence is evidenced by concrete, verifiable professional activity: a Short-Term Scientific Mission at MATE under COST Action CA22136 PANGEOS (2025); three Erasmus+ staff-mobility grants to MATE and to the University of Novi Sad (2025–2026); participation in the KP-06-COST/2 project on satellite- and UAV-based monitoring of vegetable crops for precision agriculture, with the Space Research and Technology Institute of the Bulgarian Academy of Sciences; a UAV pilot licence (A1/A3, Civil Aviation Administration of Bulgaria); membership of COST Actions CA22136 PANGEOS, CA22149 AI4Insect and CA22141 REcrop; and an MSc in Environmental Engineering (2025–2026) undertaken specifically to reskill toward the environmental-data side of the work. Her own initial development of the *DrR - Digital Agronomist* research prototype — which already integrates soil-sensor, field-meteorological and Sentinel-2 data in a common environment (§1.1.4) — is the strongest single demonstration that she can carry a biologically motivated idea into working geospatial software. In parallel, a period as a Data Analyst at KPMG Global Hungary (2024) gives her applied, non-academic data-analysis experience outside the university sector. Taken together, these are the appropriate building blocks of a plant physiologist who is deliberately extending into geospatial data science; the proposal presents them as an emerging strength supported by applied practice, mobilities and a UAV competence rather than as a mature independent publication line, which is the accurate and evaluable characterisation.

### 1.4.3 Appropriateness: an existing foundation and a precisely diagnosed development need

The appropriateness of the profile to the project follows from the fit between what the applicant already holds and what the fellowship must add. She brings the physiological, horticultural and agronomic understanding, the water-stress experimentation and physiological-phenotyping experience, the hyperspectral field-measurement practice and the prototype that the host's remote-sensing group does not itself possess (§1.3); the host supplies the scaling, Bayesian and spatio-temporal modelling, uncertainty quantification, domain adaptation and decision-evaluation competences she does not yet hold. The remaining development need is therefore not diffuse but precisely bounded — Bayesian modelling, spatio-temporal AI, sensor-domain transfer, uncertainty, domain adaptation and decision evaluation — and the intended trajectory is explicit: from Plant Physiologist/Agronomist, through EO/Geospatial Crop Scientist, to an independent researcher in transferable agricultural intelligence. A candidate who already commanded the whole method chain would not need the fellowship; a candidate without the biological foundation could not credibly acquire it in the time available. The applicant sits at exactly the point where an MSCA Postdoctoral Fellowship adds the most value.

Her experience also de-risks the practical execution of the action. She has prior, direct contact with the host and with the primary data environment: an Erasmus master's mobility at Eötvös Loránd University (ELTE), Budapest (2026), and the Short-Term Scientific Mission at MATE (2025), so integration into the ELTE remote-sensing group and access to the MATE experimental environment build on relationships that already exist rather than on introductions still to be made. Five years of university teaching at Agricultural University – Plovdiv (2015–2020) — syllabus design, lecturing and examining in Bulgarian and English including for Erasmus students, and supervision of Bachelor's theses — evidence a transferable-skills base (communication, mentoring, teaching) that the action redeploys into a new discipline, institution and language of instruction (§1.3), and her farmer-facing advisory work and her non-academic data-analyst experience evidence the inter-sectoral readiness the placement builds on. A career break for full-time parenting (2021–2024), spent in Budapest, is declared transparently in Part A and does not count against the research-experience ceiling; it is noted here only to explain the shape of the CV. Finally, the applicant is a credible near-threshold candidate rather than an untested one: her previous submission with the same host, PLANTDIGISENSE (HORIZON-MSCA-2025-PF), scored 70.40% against the 70.00% threshold, so FIELDWISE is a considered resubmission by a researcher whose readiness has already been externally assessed as fundable and whose profile the present proposal sharpens rather than assembles from scratch. On the balance of a strong, directly relevant scientific foundation, a demonstrable and applied trajectory into the project's technical methods, a precisely diagnosed and fillable competence gap, and established relationships with the host and partners, the researcher's professional experience, competences and skills are of high quality and are well matched to the demands of the proposed research.

claim_statuses.claim_summary: ~30% of EU territory is affected by seasonal water scarcity in an average year, and climate change is expected to intensify drought and irrigation demand, framing the European challenge FIELDWISE addresses.

FIELDWISE uses processing tomato as its model crop because it is a demanding predictive-irrigation system dependent on temporal interactions of water, atmospheric demand, developmental stage and management.

Central research question: whether physiologically grounded water stress in processing tomato can be forecast early enough to support irrigation decisions while retaining reliable performance across seasons, Hungary-to-Bulgaria, and research-to-commercial fields.

State-of-the-art critique: agricultural ML is predominantly evaluated by retrospective metrics (R2, RMSE, F1, accuracy) and can score well retrospectively while being unsuitable for irrigation management (data leakage, environment-specific learning, late detection, commercial-field failure).
The six research and innovation objectives O1–O6 with their canonical titles and measurable targets.
Objectives are verified by the named deliverables D1.1/D1.2 (month 6), D2.1/D2.2 (month 14), D3.1/D3.2 (month 18), D4.1/D4.2/D4.3 (month 21), D5.1 (month 24), and D5.2/D5.3/D5.4/D5.5 (month 30).

The objectives decompose into seven research questions RQ1–RQ7 and six hypotheses H1–H6, with H3–H6 framed as performance changes to be quantified (temporal, geographic and operational degradation; accuracy not equal to decision value).
Six scientific gaps G1–G6 (physiological-target, sensor-domain, temporal, geographic-transferability, operational-transferability, decision-value) are stated and map to the objectives.

Ambition is expressed as six transitions (spectral proxy to physiological target; hyperspectral discovery to satellite scaling; static detection to prospective prediction; internal validation to temporal transferability; single-country to geographic transferability; research accuracy to commercial-field decision value) and a four-stage validation ladder.

FIELDWISE establishes a methodological bridge from high-information proximal hyperspectral observation to scalable Sentinel-2 prediction, and defines stress physiologically rather than by spectral proxy.
Field Decision Value (FDV) is introduced as a final evaluation layer so models are selected by field-level irrigation usefulness rather than retrospective accuracy alone.
Five work packages WP1–WP5 (canonical titles) instantiate the design with a WP1->WP2->WP3->WP4->WP5 dependency chain.

A DrR - Digital Agronomist desktop research prototype already exists and demonstrates integration of soil-sensor, field-meteorological and Sentinel-2 data; FIELDWISE supplies the missing scientific validation and transferability framework rather than converting the prototype into a website.
Achievability rests on an existing five-year MATE archive (harmonisation rather than new multi-year collection) so principal risks are scientific rather than infrastructural.
The action runs 30 months: a 24-month European Fellowship (M1–M24) plus a 6-month non-academic placement (M25–M30); the web MVP (D5.1) at month 24 precedes the placement.

The design responds to prior-submission criticisms: methodological treatment of heterogeneous spatial/spectral/temporal information, milestone/corrective-action timing, and substantiation of the route to users and IP strategy.

Strategic differentiation moves agricultural AI from retrospective accuracy toward temporal, geographic and operational transferability and decision value, expressed as six transitions and a four-step validation ladder.
The project title is 'Beyond Prediction Accuracy: From Transferable Crop Water-Stress Forecasts to Field-Level Irrigation Decisions'.

The overall methodology is a four-stage transferability validation ladder (MATE scientific development/validation -> MVCRI cross-country transferability -> AgroVIR operational transferability -> DrR Web MVP research-to-operation delivery), instantiated as five work packages with the stated dependency chain.
Work stress is defined through a physiologically grounded target replacing spectral-proxy definitions (WP1 task Establish physiological stress definition; gap G1; transition TR1).
A leakage-safe validation design is established in WP1 and delivered as the Data/target/validation protocol due in month 6, constraining downstream modelling.

The sensor-domain bridge from proximal hyperspectral to Sentinel-2 uses spectral-response resampling, concurrent proximal/satellite observation and spatial-scale calibration (WP2 tasks), delivered as the Hyperspectral-to-Sentinel transfer library due in month 14.

The prediction layer uses temporal feature engineering, transparent baselines, RF/XGBoost, Bayesian/hierarchical models, multi-horizon forecasting, probability calibration and uncertainty quantification, and feature ablation/error analysis (WP3 tasks).
The underpinning assumptions are stated as six falsifiable hypotheses H1-H6, several framed as performance degradations to be quantified rather than confirmed.

Field Decision Value (FDV) is established in WP5 as the final evaluation layer selecting models by field-level irrigation usefulness (lead time, calibration, avoided false/missed interventions) rather than retrospective accuracy; delivered as the Field Decision Value report due in month 30.

The methodology rests on an existing approximately five-year MATE archive (harmonised, not newly collected) and the DrR - Digital Agronomist desktop research prototype, making residual risks scientific rather than infrastructural.
Objective-to-work-package mapping (O1<-WP1, O2<-WP2, O3<-WP3, O4<-WP4, O5/O6<-WP5), each closed by named deliverables with the stated due months.

Deliverable titles and due months (D1.1/D1.2 month 6, D2.1/D2.2 month 14, D3.1/D3.2 month 18, D4.1/D4.2/D4.3 month 21, D5.1 month 24, D5.2-D5.5 month 30; D1.3 Career Development Plan agreed by month 3).

The five identified methodological challenges (data leakage, sensor-domain scale gap, limited sample/temporal density, cross-country transfer failure, commercial-field heterogeneity) each have a mitigation built into the work plan (leave-one-year-out validation, concurrent observation/scale calibration, graded model portfolio, zero-shot transfer plus limited Bulgarian calibration and hierarchical adaptation, operational transfer with robustness identification).
The architecture directly responds to a previous submission's identified weakness in the methodological treatment of heterogeneous spatial, spectral and temporal information.

An interdisciplinary approach is necessary because the central question spans plant physiology, remote sensing, geoinformatics/EO, machine learning/uncertainty, and operational decision support; no single discipline answers it.

The integrated disciplines and their carriers: supervisor Prof. Andras Jung (remote sensing, hyperspectral imaging, field spectroscopy, geoinformatics) and co-supervisor Dr. Roland Hollos (machine learning and meta-modelling, agro-meteorology) providing the methodological lead and quality assurance for model development and testing.

Integration is realised structurally (the fellow, a single researcher, executes all five work packages, with two-way transfer of knowledge between crop physiology/agronomy and geospatial data science), through supervision (division of methodological responsibility and QA), and through governance (the Project Steering Group coordinating host, MATE, MVCRI and AgroVIR).

A biological sex/gender dimension is not relevant to the core research content because the subject is a crop (processing tomato) with no human/animal subject in the modelled system; justification provided per the guidance.

Relevant diversity aspects are addressed through agro-environmental/geographic diversity (Hungary MATE, Bulgaria MVCRI, commercial AgroVIR fields) and, where human participants provide structured feedback in WP5, inclusive engagement under informed consent with no special-category data and aggregated/anonymised reporting.

Personal data (MVP user/farm details, field boundaries) and commercially sensitive farmer data are handled under GDPR data minimisation, DPO review and a data-sharing agreement, with results published only in aggregated or anonymised form.

Open science is implemented as an integral part of the methodology under 'as open as possible, as closed as necessary', producing harmonisation protocols, validation split manifests, hyperspectral-to-Sentinel methodology, code where IP permits, model cards, FAIR metadata, anonymised derived datasets and open-access publications; open-science engagement is also a named Career Development Plan component.
The call mandates that training/research activities foster an open-science culture, knowledge valorisation and research integrity, which the methodology's open-science practices satisfy.
A Data Management Plan will be produced as an early deliverable by month 6, defining FAIR handling, access conditions, retention and licensing, and the open/restricted boundary.
Cross-country measurements at MVCRI are collected under a pre-registered protocol, supporting reproducibility.

Two open-science constraints are stated: some code is subject to the background IP of the pre-existing DrR components, and some farmer data is commercially sensitive, invoking 'as closed as necessary' while still opening methodology, metadata and anonymised derivatives.

Training is organised through the Career Development Plan (D1.3), agreed by month 3, signed by both supervisors and the fellow, and reviewed at the project's five steering points.

Eleven host-to-fellow scientific competences (geoinformatics; EO time-series; optical/SAR integration; hyperspectral-to-multispectral transfer; spatio-temporal modelling; Bayesian hierarchical modelling; uncertainty quantification; transfer learning/domain adaptation; reproducible geospatial computation; research software/web deployment; IP and research exploitation) map onto the fellow's competence gap.

Seven transferable/management-skill strands trained: research integrity; open science and FAIR practice; generative-AI literacy; grant writing; IP and exploitation; project management; science communication.

The transferable-skills training satisfies the call requirement (SR-04) to integrate transferable skills including generative AI and foster open science, knowledge valorisation and research integrity.

The two-way transfer strengthens the host's R&I capacity and knowledge-transfer capability (EO-07) and the supervision quality outcome (EO-05).

The placement supplies inter-sectoral competences (operational AI evaluation, research-to-MVP translation, commercial agricultural-software requirements) the academic host cannot provide, improving employability in precision-agriculture, irrigation-technology and FMIS companies.
